name: Grace Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Grace, I'm 27, and I'm a video and social reporter at a regional digital news brand called Metro North. We don't print anything; it's all phone video, short clips and the website. I live alone in a studio flat by the tram stop, and I do freelance filming for local cafés and gyms on weekends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out most mornings with my phone on a little stabiliser, filming whatever's happening: a protest at the town hall, a burst water main, a new bakery queue. I use AI every day to caption clips, cut them to vertical, and translate the subtitles for our audiences who speak other languages. I love being first on the scene and getting it up in twenty minutes. What wears me out is that my scripts are still weak, so my editor, Callum, often re-voices my clips himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not shocked, because the tools are good at fiddly jobs and bad at judgement. I'd post a short clip about it, probably filmed on the tram. At work I'd say let's keep using what works and stop talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a good world for me. The tools already save me hours on captions and edits, and Metro North's audience is growing while the old papers shrink. My freelance work brings in an extra few hundred a month on top, so money's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and spend more time on my scripts, maybe a short presenting course. I'd push my freelance work a bit further, say one more regular client. And I'd keep my savings around three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. If AI never gets smarter than my captioning app, I'm the reporter who already knows how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, a bit, in the sense that he could get fed up re-voicing my clips. That's on me to fix. And brands like ours depend on the big video apps, which change their rules whenever they like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the freelance work matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a cushion and it's fun. A café pays me 150 for a month of clips, a gym pays a bit more. If Metro North ever went wobbly, it would be a start.

say: I'd say the tools are good at **fiddly jobs**, bad at judgement.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep using what works** and move on.
think: I think this world is **good for me**, with a growing audience.
My **freelance work** adds a few hundred a month.
do: Take a short **presenting course** to fix weak scripts.
S0.quote: If AI never gets smarter than my captioning app, I'm the reporter who already knows how to use it.
fieldNote: Grace feels **secure**: her outlet is growing and she has side income.
She's honest that her **scripts** are weak and sees it as hers to fix.
Her only worry is **platform rules** set by the big video apps.

steps.text: Keep using AI for captions, edits and subtitles
Sign up one more café or gym as a freelance client
Take a short presenting course to fix weak scripts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so learn it, and I'd make a few clips showing how. At work I'd be the one helping people set things up. I'd try not to be smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay for a while, but the bits I'm bad at, scripts and voice-overs, are exactly what the software would do. So my weak spot stops mattering, and the thing I'm good at, being there with a camera, matters more. The risk is Metro North deciding to use people's own footage and AI to do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new editing and script tools fast, before anyone asked. I'd build the freelance side into a proper small business, with a simple website and a rate card. And I'd buy a better camera and microphone, maybe 800 pounds, because real footage looks different from fake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and a bit wary. I like change, but I can see where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said real footage looks different. Will people still care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some won't, but the local ones will. People in my town can tell when a video was actually filmed on their own high street and when a computer made it up. That's my bet, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Metro North would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two writers who do the text versions of stories. Their whole job is rewriting what's in the video into words, and software already does a rough version. They're nice, and they're older than me, and they don't film.

say: I'd say AI is here, so **learn it**, and show people how.
I'd be the one **helping colleagues** set things up.
think: I think my **weak scripts** stop mattering as software does them.
Being there **with a camera** matters more.
do: Learn the new **editing tools** before being asked.
Turn freelance work into a **small business** with a rate card.
Buy a **better camera** and microphone for about 800.
S1.quote: People in my town can tell when a video was actually filmed on their own high street and when a computer made it up.
fieldNote: Grace sees her **on-scene filming** as her edge as writing gets automated.
She worries for the **text writers** who rewrite videos into words.
She'd **invest** in kit, betting that real local footage keeps its value.

steps.text: Learn the new AI editing and script tools early
Set up a website and rate card for freelance filming
Buy a better camera and microphone for about 800 pounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge, and I'd try to explain it simply, because that's my job. I'd film people talking about what it means for them. I wouldn't pretend to know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my staff job goes. Metro North would get AI to write, voice and edit everything, and pay people with phones for raw footage. I'm good at being first to a burst water main with my phone, and by 2028 that's about all a newsroom would still need me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd put more money aside, cancel the extras, and push the freelance work hard. I'd sign up local businesses for filmed events, weddings, openings, where someone still has to stand there with a camera until the robots arrive around 2031. And I'd think about what comes after that, maybe event organising, where you deal with people face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, under all the planning. I'd be planning so I didn't have to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said until the robots arrive. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then even the filming goes, I suppose. I'd have three years of freelance money and contacts. Three years of weddings and shop openings is a short runway, but it's longer than my staff job would get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second streaming account and the gym, then my weekend trips. I wouldn't cut kit, because that's how I earn. Rent's the big one and I can't do much about it in a studio this small.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and try to explain it simply.
I'd film people talking about what it **means for them**.
think: I think my **staff job** goes as AI writes, voices and edits.
Being **first on scene** would be my only remaining value.
do: Cut **extras** and add to savings straight away.
Sell filming for **weddings and openings** to local businesses.
S2.quote: I'm good at being first to a burst water main with my phone, and by 2028 that's about all a newsroom would still need me for.
fieldNote: Grace expects to **lose her staff job** but sees a three-year window for filming.
She plans hard and admits she does it to **avoid the fear**.
She protects her **kit**, treating it as her livelihood.

steps.text: Cancel the second streaming account and the gym
Sell event filming to wedding venues and new shops
Look into event organising work for after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be smart about it. I'd make a short series on people changing careers. I'd be upbeat but honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough to build a proper business. I'd still lose the staff job, probably around 2030. But I'd be 32, with a client list, and with the robot gap I'd have filming work till about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This first year I'd grow the freelance side to five regular clients and register as a small business. I'd stay at Metro North while it lasts, using every tool to be the fastest on the desk. And I'd start a short course in event management in year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and excited at once. It's a gamble I'd actually want to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. What's the part that isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, if I'm honest. Three months of savings isn't much if I go full freelance. I'd want six before leaving the staff job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger reporter in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to film, learn to talk to people, and learn the tools. Don't just learn to write. A reporter who can only write is in trouble, and a reporter who can turn up and film is in trouble a few years later.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so people should be smart about it.
I'd make an upbeat but honest series on **career changes**.
think: I think five years is enough for a **proper business**.
With the robot gap I'd have **filming work** until about 2034.
do: Start an **event management** course in year two.
S3.quote: A reporter who can only write is in trouble, and a reporter who can turn up and film is in trouble a few years later.
fieldNote: Grace treats five years as a chance to **build a business** before the staff job ends.
She's honest that **savings** are too thin to go freelance yet.
She sees the robot gap as **extra years** for filming work.

steps.text: Grow the freelance filming to five regular clients
Save up to six months before leaving the staff job
Start an event management course in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so the media should stop panicking. I'd keep making clips explaining it. People like a calm voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good about this one. I'd have years to get better at presenting and build the business. By 2036 I'd have a name locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Metro North and keep using the tools every day. I'd grow the freelance side steadily, not in a rush. And I'd keep an eye on how fast the tools improve each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of a buzz, too, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret doing too slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, probably. With ten years of warning, my only real excuse for being caught short would be spending everything on camera kit. I'd set up an automatic transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know it was time to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Metro North stopped hiring juniors. That's always the first sign. I'd watch the job ads like a hawk.

say: I'd say ten years is **loads of time** and the media should stop panicking.
I'd keep making **clips** that explain it calmly.
think: I think I'd feel **pretty good** about this one.
By 2036 I'd have a **local name** and years of presenting practice.
do: Stay at Metro North and use the **tools daily**.
Set up an **automatic transfer** into savings.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a bit of a **buzz**.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, my only real excuse for being caught short would be spending everything on camera kit.
fieldNote: Grace feels **in control** with ten years, though she still watches the signs.
Her named warning sign is Metro North **no longer hiring juniors**.
She knows her weakness is **spending on kit** rather than saving.

steps.text: Stay at Metro North as video reporter
Use AI daily for captions and edits
Set up an automatic monthly transfer into savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years of filming and then nothing, with no time to build anything. What would help is cheap business support for freelancers and training in face-to-face work, like event management.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. When anyone can fake a video of my high street, the most valuable thing I own is that people know I was really there.

headlineQuote: When anyone can fake a video of my high street, the most valuable thing I own is that people know I was really there.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** video and social reporter at a growing digital news brand.
She uses AI **every day** and feels secure in the mild pictures.
Her weak spot is **scripts**, and her strength is being first on scene with a camera.
She builds **freelance filming** as her backup, betting on the gap before robots arrive.
Fast AGI frightens her; slower versions feel like a **gamble** she'd enjoy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have only three years of filming work left.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **business support** for freelancers and training in **face-to-face** work.
